summary: Dengue is a viral infection spread by Aedes mosquito bites. Many people have mild illness, but some develop severe dengue, which can become dangerous around the time the fever settles.
causes: Dengue virus transmitted by Aedes aegypti / Aedes albopictus mosquitoes (they bite mainly during the day).
risk_factors: Living in or travelling to areas with dengue cases, especially in and after the monsoon
Stagnant clean water near home (coolers, containers, tyres)
Previous dengue infection (risk of severe dengue on a second infection)
Infants, older adults, pregnancy and people with other chronic illness may need closer monitoring

tests.name: NS1 antigen test
tests.purpose: Detects the virus early in the illness.

preparation.other: Most useful in the first few days of fever (roughly the first 5 days).

tests.exceptions: A negative early test does not rule out dengue; the doctor may repeat or use another test.

tests.name: Dengue IgM/IgG antibody test

preparation.other: Becomes useful later in the illness (roughly after day 5).

tests.exceptions: Antibodies can also reflect older infection; interpretation by a doctor is needed.

tests.name: CBC with platelet count and haematocrit
tests.purpose: Helps the doctor monitor the illness; counts may be repeated.

preparation.other: Preparation can differ between labs and between patients; follow the instructions of your doctor or lab.

tests.exceptions: Platelet count alone does not decide severity; the doctor looks at the whole clinical picture.

prevention: Remove or cover stagnant water; empty and dry coolers, pots and containers weekly
Use mosquito nets, repellents and full-sleeve clothing, including during the day
lifestyle: Rest and drink plenty of safe fluids as advised by the doctor
Avoid aspirin and ibuprofen-type painkillers unless a doctor specifically advises them (bleeding risk)
Do not self-medicate; follow the doctor's monitoring schedule
red_flags: Persistent vomiting or unable to drink fluids
Bleeding from nose or gums, blood in vomit or black stools
Cold, clammy skin, difficulty breathing, very little urine
These warning signs often appear when the fever is settling (about day 3 to 7) and need urgent hospital care
when_to_consult: Fever with body ache or rash in a dengue season or area: see a doctor early rather than waiting
Any warning sign above: go to hospital immediately
special_populations: Children and infants: see a paediatrician early
Pregnancy: consult a doctor promptly if dengue is suspected
Older adults and people with diabetes, heart or kidney disease need closer supervision

faqs.q: Can a normal platelet count rule out dengue?
faqs.a: No single test rules dengue in or out. Doctors combine symptoms, day of illness and test results.

faqs.q: Should I take papaya leaf juice or home remedies instead of seeing a doctor?
faqs.a: No. Home remedies should not replace medical monitoring, because dengue can worsen suddenly.

summary: Malaria is a parasite infection spread by Anopheles mosquito bites. It causes fever that may come with chills and sweating. It needs a blood test and proper treatment; it can become severe if delayed.
causes: Plasmodium parasites passed on by infected Anopheles mosquitoes.
risk_factors: Living in or travelling to areas with malaria
Stagnant water and poor mosquito protection
Pregnancy and young children are at higher risk of severe illness

tests.name: Rapid diagnostic test (RDT) and/or blood smear microscopy
tests.purpose: Confirms malaria and identifies the parasite type, which decides treatment.

preparation.other: Best done while symptoms are present and before antimalarial medicine is started.

tests.exceptions: One negative test during fever does not always exclude malaria; the doctor may repeat it.

prevention: Use repellents and cover arms and legs in the evening
Remove stagnant water around the home
lifestyle: Treatment depends on the parasite type, so do not take leftover or self-chosen medicines
Drink fluids and rest as the doctor advises
red_flags: Yellow eyes or skin, or very dark urine
Persistent vomiting or unable to drink
Pregnancy with fever in a malaria area
when_to_consult: Any fever with chills, especially after mosquito exposure or travel, should be tested
special_populations: Pregnancy and children: seek medical care without delay
Travellers returning from malaria areas should mention travel history to the doctor

faqs.q: Is fever with chills always malaria?
faqs.a: No. Several infections can cause this pattern; a blood test is needed to know.
